entities.summary:
Arnoul d'Audrehem (died 1 December 1370), a prominent Marshal of France during the tumultuous mid-14th century, epitomized the martial spirit and evolving diplomatic complexities of the Hundred Years' War. Originating from Audrehem in Artois, his career spanned pivotal military campaigns and sensitive diplomatic missions for Kings John II and Charles V, making him a central figure in the Anglo-French conflict and a testament to the shifting roles of medieval aristocracy in warfare and statecraft.

d'Audrehem's career was marked by significant military engagements and periods of captivity. He served with distinction in various theaters, participating in the Battle of Poitiers in 1356 where he was captured alongside King John II. Following his release, he engaged in campaigns against the Free Companies plaguing France and led expeditions into Navarre and Aragon in the 1360s, notably commanding forces in support of Henry of Trastámara against Peter the Cruel. His strategic acumen was recognized by Charles V, who utilized him not only as a field commander but also as a crucial negotiator, particularly during the peace talks that led to the Treaty of Brétigny in 1360.

His contributions extended beyond the battlefield; d'Audrehem played a role in the professionalization of the French military command and the development of more coherent strategic responses to the English threat and internal brigandage. His diplomatic efforts, though not always conclusive, reflected the intricate network of alliances and rivalries that characterized late medieval Europe, influencing the geopolitical landscape of the Iberian Peninsula and the ongoing Anglo-French struggle. He represented a transitional figure, bridging the gap between traditional feudal levies and a more organized, state-controlled military apparatus.
